prompt: What is wrong with "storage is cheap, so collect everything now and decide what it is for later"?
hint: Storage is not the only thing a row costs.

choices.text: Every row must also be moved, checked, read and protected
choices.why: Right: storage is the cheap part of a promise kept every day.

choices.text: Storage is in fact expensive, and the phrase hides it
choices.why: Storage is cheap; the section agrees with that half.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the data is semi-structured
choices.why: The shape of the data changes none of the costs around it.

choices.text: It only fails for data about bicycles and docks
choices.why: It fails hardest for data about people, which also needs a purpose.

prompt: Caio asks for every dock's reading, every minute, kept for good. What does Davi ask him first?
hint: Every other answer depends on it.

choices.text: Which file format he would like the readings in
choices.why: A format is chosen once the use is known.

choices.text: How much free disk his laptop has for them
choices.why: Where they go comes after what they are for.

choices.text: What the model is for
choices.why: Right: "how fresh" and "how much" mean nothing until that is said.

choices.text: Whether he can wait for a warehouse to be built
choices.why: That is a delivery question, and it comes after the purpose.

prompt: Why are volume, frequency, quality and cost asked together, before the first copy?
hint: Change one answer and look at the others.

choices.text: A regulator requires all four to be answered in writing
choices.why: Writing them down is good practice, not a regulation about these four.

choices.text: The tools for all four are bought from one vendor together
choices.why: No tool is being bought here; the questions come before tools.

choices.text: Once data is personal, the privacy question replaces the four
choices.why: Privacy sits underneath the four; it replaces none of them.

choices.text: Each answer moves the others, so none is settled on its own
choices.why: Right: frequency multiplies runs, volume and reads multiply the bill.

prompt: How many bytes a row did the one-hour sample of dock readings measure, in JSON Lines?
hint: The first line `volume.py` prints.

prompt: The values in one reading add up to 39 characters, yet a row measured more than twice that. Why?
hint: Look at the first line of the sample.

choices.text: Python pads each value to a fixed width when writing JSON
choices.why: JSON has no fixed widths; the line shows no padding.

choices.text: Every line repeats the key names, with their quotes and colons
choices.why: Right: names, quotes and colons, on every one of the 9000 lines.

choices.text: The voltage is stored with far more decimals than it shows
choices.why: It is rounded to two decimals before it is written.

choices.text: The file starts with a header line that is far longer than the rows
choices.why: JSON Lines has no header; that is exactly why each line names its fields.

prompt: How should the bytes a row be estimated before collecting a source?
hint: The guess is the number to distrust.

choices.text: Add up the characters of the values each row carries
choices.why: That was the guess of about forty, less than half the real size.

choices.text: Multiply the number of fields by a typical eight bytes
choices.why: A rule of thumb ignores the format, which is most of the size.

choices.text: Ask the source for the typical size of its rows
choices.why: The source knows its own format, not the one you will store.

choices.text: Measure a sample written the way it will be stored
choices.why: Right: write it the way it will be kept, then divide.

prompt: With the eight new stations of twelve docks each, how many readings a day will the sensors send?
hint: 246 docks, one reading a minute each.

prompt: What does an estimate of 8.1 GB a year tell Davi about the tools the sensor data needs?
hint: Compare it with the disk of an ordinary laptop.

choices.text: A cluster is needed from the first day
choices.why: A cluster is for data that no longer fits on one machine; lesson 9.

choices.text: One machine is enough
choices.why: Right: it fits on a laptop, and the standard library handles it.

choices.text: Only a sample can be kept, never the whole year
choices.why: The whole year fits easily; nothing has to be thrown away.

choices.text: A columnar warehouse is the only place that can hold it
choices.why: A few gigabytes fit anywhere; the format is a separate choice.

prompt: Caio needs readings minute by minute, delivered once a week. Which of the two words describes "minute by minute"?
hint: One is how fine the record is; the other is how old it may be.

choices.text: Freshness
choices.why: Freshness is the once a week: how old the newest data may be.

choices.text: Granularity
choices.why: Right: how finely the data records what happened.

choices.text: Both at once
choices.why: They are different things, which is the point of the section.

prompt: Polling every minute for a day makes 1,440 calls. How many came back empty in `poll.py`?
hint: The `empty` column, first row.

prompt: What does polling cost that push avoids?
hint: Think about the night.

choices.text: Calls that find nothing, and the wait until the next one
choices.why: Right: push sends each record when it happens, so neither exists.

choices.text: A copy of the source kept on your side
choices.why: Both ways end with a copy; that is what collecting is.

choices.text: The need for the source to offer it
choices.why: That is push's price, not polling's: polling needs only answers.

choices.text: Records lost while your side is down
choices.why: That is push's risk; a poll simply asks again later.

prompt: Match each reader to how fresh its data has to be.
hint: Ask what each one does with the data.

pairs.left: the app's map of free bicycles

pairs.right: the last full week, by Sunday night

prompt: Why is "real time" the wrong first answer to "how fresh must it be"?
hint: Ask what decision changes.

choices.text: Real-time data is less accurate than data copied in batches
choices.why: Accuracy and freshness are separate; the issue is cost.

choices.text: No source in practice can send data within a minute of it happening
choices.why: The sensors do, to the app. It can be had; the question is whether it is needed.

choices.text: It is asked for before anyone checks what would change
choices.why: Right: fresher costs more, and only a decision that changes pays for it.

choices.text: The LGPD forbids collecting personal data as it happens
choices.why: The law is about purpose and necessity, not about timing.

prompt: In an incremental load, the newest change the previous run saw is stored as the ___.
hint: A word borrowed from the mark a river leaves.

prompt: Why did the copy with no overlap never get `R000041`?
hint: Compare its `updated_at` with the watermark.

choices.text: Its transaction failed and the source rolled it back
choices.why: It committed at 10:01, and `compare.py` finds it in the source.

choices.text: Its stamp, 09:57, was below the watermark the first copy had saved
choices.why: Right: it committed after the 10:00 copy, and later runs start above 09:59.

choices.text: `INSERT OR REPLACE` wrote the refund over it
choices.why: The refund is `R000010`; a different key replaces nothing here.

choices.text: The copy ran before the morning rides existed
choices.why: The first run copied all forty morning rides.

prompt: Both copies picked up the refund of `R000010`, an old ride. Why?
hint: What happens to `updated_at` when a row changes?

choices.text: The refund moved its `updated_at` forward to 10:02, above the watermark
choices.why: Right: a change to an old row is a new time, above the watermark.

choices.text: Every run copies refunds in full, whatever their time
choices.why: The query asks only for `updated_at` above `since`; it knows no refunds.

choices.text: The overlap of ten minutes reached back to its ride at 08:29
choices.why: The copy with no overlap caught it too.

choices.text: `compare.py` repaired both copies after they had run
choices.why: `compare.py` only reads; it writes nothing.

prompt: In its second run, how many rows did the copy with ten minutes of overlap read?
hint: `read ... rows since 09:49`.

prompt: The overlap reads some rows a second time. What keeps those rows from appearing twice in the copy?
hint: Look at how the copy writes.

choices.text: The watermark skipping the rows it has already seen once
choices.why: The overlap exists precisely to read some of them again.

choices.text: SQLite refusing any row it has received before
choices.why: SQLite stores what it is told; the program decides it replaces.

choices.text: An overlap kept shorter than one hour
choices.why: Any overlap re-reads rows; the length decides how many, not whether they double.

choices.text: Writes keyed on `ride_id`, replacing the old
choices.why: Right: `INSERT OR REPLACE` by key makes a second read harmless.

prompt: Which of these can a ten-minute overlap NOT catch? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what has an `updated_at` inside the window.

choices.text: A row deleted in the source
choices.why: Yes: a deleted row has no `updated_at` left to find.

choices.text: A row stamped by a server whose clock is a day slow
choices.why: Yes: a day is far outside ten minutes.

choices.text: A row whose commit was two minutes late
choices.why: No: that is the case the overlap is for.

choices.text: A refund of a ride from last week
choices.why: No: the refund moves `updated_at` to now.

prompt: Put the steps of one incremental run in order.
hint: The watermark is saved last.
items: ask for rows changed after it, minus the overlap
write them into the copy by key
trap: Saving the watermark before the commit loses the rows of a run that dies halfway.

prompt: The delivery for the 16th has 137 rows where the source says it sent 200. What does the door do?
hint: It is a check on the file.

choices.text: Loads the 137, since each passes the row checks
choices.why: That makes the day look quiet: a wrong number, not a missing one.

choices.text: Loads them and puts the 63 missing ones in quarantine
choices.why: Missing rows cannot be quarantined; they are not there.

choices.text: Refuses the whole file, and the program ends with an error
choices.why: Right: nothing is loaded, and a scheduler sees the failure.

choices.text: Loads the rows and flags the day as partial in a column
choices.why: Every reader would have to remember to check the flag.

prompt: Match each quarantined row of the 15th to the kind of check that caught it.
hint: Four rows, four kinds.

prompt: Why is a row that fails a check quarantined instead of dropped?
hint: Who finds out it existed?

choices.text: So it can be loaded automatically the next night
choices.why: Nothing in it is fixed by waiting a night.

choices.text: So somebody can see it, and why
choices.why: Right: a silent drop is invisible to every report.

choices.text: Because the LGPD forbids deleting any data that has arrived
choices.why: The LGPD in fact requires deleting personal data on request.

choices.text: Because the row count would no longer match the source
choices.why: The count is checked on the file before any row is judged.

prompt: The delivery of the 15th had 200 rows and passed the file checks, yet `R000151` was not in it. Which check at the door could have noticed?
hint: The file kept its promised count.

choices.text: The uniqueness check, which flagged `R000150` instead
choices.why: It saw the double, not what the double replaced.

choices.text: The row count, compared with the 200 promised
choices.why: The count was 200: one doubled, one missing.

choices.text: None of them: the file had all 200 rows it promised
choices.why: Right: only the source's own list of rides shows it; that is reconciliation.

choices.text: The reference check on the start station
choices.why: It judges the rows that are there, not the ones that are not.

prompt: A quarantine file has grown by four hundred rows a day for a week, and nobody has opened it. What has happened, in effect?
hint: Where are those rows in Marta's report?

choices.text: A silent drop of rows, and a source that has changed
choices.why: Right: four hundred a day is a change, and an unread quarantine hides it.

choices.text: Quality improved, since the bad rows were kept out
choices.why: Rows kept out with nobody looking are rows missing from every number.

choices.text: Nothing yet: quarantined rows load once the source fixes them
choices.why: Nobody told the source; nothing will fix them.

choices.text: The whole delivery was refused each day, so nothing loaded
choices.why: Refusal is for file checks; quarantine means the rest did load.

prompt: A row that fails a check at the door is set aside in ___, with its reason.
hint: A word from medicine: kept apart until it is safe.

prompt: Where must the second number in a reconciliation come from?
hint: A number that agrees by construction proves nothing.

choices.text: The pipeline's own count of the copy it made
choices.why: That agrees with the copy whatever the copy holds.

choices.text: Yesterday's reconciliation, carried forward a day
choices.why: Yesterday says nothing about what arrived today.

choices.text: The number of lines in the quarantine file
choices.why: Quarantine counts rejects, not what the source holds.

choices.text: The source, from its own record of what it holds
choices.why: Right: a statement, a count on a replica, the number beside a file.

prompt: On 2025-09-19, how many payments did each side count?
hint: Both sides agree on it.

prompt: The 19th passed on count and failed on sum. What happened?
hint: The keys say it.

choices.text: One payment arrived twice and another never did
choices.why: Right: `P19005` twice, `P19030` never, and their amounts differ.

choices.text: The provider rounded its amounts to whole reais
choices.why: Both sides are in centavos; nothing was rounded.

choices.text: A payment's amount was altered on the way in
choices.why: The keys show a double and a gap, not an edited amount.

choices.text: The two sides closed the day at different hours
choices.why: That would shift payments every day, not only the 19th.

prompt: Put the three levels of reconciliation in order, from the cheapest to the most thorough.
hint: One number a day, then two, then every key.
trap: Keys find exactly which rows, and need every key from both sides.

prompt: In `cost.py`, what does the dashboard reading the whole year cost a month, in reais?
hint: The fourth line of costs.

prompt: The same dashboard costs R$ 5.75 a month when it reads only today. What made the difference?
hint: Nothing about the data changed.

choices.text: Today's data compresses much better than a year of it
choices.why: The program applies no compression; it divides by 365.

choices.text: Query engines charge less for data written recently
choices.why: One price per terabyte is used for both lines.

choices.text: It refreshes once a day instead of every five minutes
choices.why: Both lines use the same 8640 refreshes.

choices.text: It reads one day, not 365
choices.why: Right: same refreshes, one 365th of the bytes.

prompt: What decides whether a query for today can avoid reading the rest of the year?
hint: Lesson 3 stored its raw rides in a particular way.

choices.text: How the data was laid out when collected
choices.why: Right: one directory per day lets a query open one directory.

choices.text: The provider's price list for the region the data is in
choices.why: Prices change what a read costs, not how much is read.

choices.text: How many people have the dashboard open at once
choices.why: That multiplies the reads; it does not shrink each one.

choices.text: Whether the readings were pushed by the source or polled
choices.why: How data arrives says nothing about how it is stored.

prompt: Which of these costs grow with how often the data is read or moved? Choose all that apply.
hint: One grows with volume and time instead.

choices.text: compute, by the terabyte read
choices.why: Yes: every refresh reads again.

choices.text: transfer out of the provider
choices.why: Yes: paid again on every copy.

choices.text: calls to a paid API
choices.why: Yes: one per poll.

choices.text: storage, by the gigabyte-month
choices.why: No: it grows with volume and with every month kept.

prompt: Which LGPD principle limits personal data to the minimum its purpose requires?
hint: Article 6 names it.

choices.text: Purpose
choices.why: Purpose says what the data is for; the other one limits how much.

choices.text: Necessity
choices.why: Right: no more than the purpose requires.

choices.text: Transparency
choices.why: Transparency is about telling the person, not about how much is held.

choices.text: Security
choices.why: Security protects what is held; it does not limit it.

prompt: Why is a plain SHA-256 of a phone number not anonymous?
hint: What did the partner do?

choices.text: SHA-256 can be decrypted with the right tool
choices.why: A hash is not encryption; it is recomputed, not decrypted.

choices.text: Anyone can hash a list of numbers and compare
choices.why: Right: no secret, and only a hundred million Curitiba mobiles.

choices.text: The hash is longer than the phone number it hides
choices.why: Length has nothing to do with whether it can be linked.

choices.text: Two different phone numbers often share the same hash
choices.why: Collisions are not the problem; matching is.

prompt: How many of the partner's three numbers were found among the plain hashes?
hint: The second-to-last line of `pseudo.py`.

prompt: Caio's model needs rides per station per hour. What should happen to the exact second each ride started?
hint: Needed, but only roughly.

choices.text: Pseudonymise it with a keyed hash before copying
choices.why: A pseudonym is for telling people apart, not for a time.

choices.text: Leave the whole ride out of the copy
choices.why: The model counts rides; it needs them.

choices.text: Keep it, since a time is never personal data
choices.why: Where somebody was, and when, describes that person.

choices.text: Coarsen it to the hour
choices.why: Right: the question needs the hour, not the second.

prompt: Replacing an identifier with a consistent stand-in that only a separately kept key can link back is called ___.
hint: Not anonymisation.

prompt: Why does "what is it for?" sit first on the checklist?
hint: Try answering "how fresh?" without it.

choices.text: Because the LGPD asks that it be written first in every document
choices.why: The law asks for a purpose, not for an order on a page.

choices.text: Because it is the only question the owner can answer
choices.why: The owner answers several others; the purpose comes from the reader.

choices.text: The other answers depend on it
choices.why: Right: freshness, volume and checks mean nothing without a use.

choices.text: Because it is the quickest question on the list to answer
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; it comes first anyway.

prompt: The sensors' server keeps readings for two days. What does that make the pipeline's outages?
hint: Think of a long weekend.

choices.text: Harmless, since the copy can catch up whenever it restarts
choices.why: Only for two days; after that the readings are gone.

choices.text: A deadline: after two days down, those readings are lost for good
choices.why: Right: those readings are gone, and nobody collects them again.

choices.text: A reason to poll the server every minute
choices.why: Polling more often does not help a pipeline that is down.

choices.text: A matter for the sensors' team alone to solve
choices.why: It is a fact about the source the pipeline has to plan for.

prompt: A partner's API charges per call and can also push each event to an address you give it. Marta reads its data once a week. What fits?
hint: Who reads it, and how often?

choices.text: Polling every minute, so nothing is ever more than a minute old
choices.why: A minute of freshness that nobody reads, paid for in calls.

choices.text: Push, and a receiver running all week to listen for it
choices.why: It works, and keeps a service up all week for a weekly reader.

choices.text: One pull a week, before she reads
choices.why: Right: the reader decides the freshness, and one call a week is the cheapest.

choices.text: Polling every hour, as a compromise between the two
choices.why: A compromise between answers nobody needed is still too fresh.

prompt: One app server's clock runs three minutes slow, and it stamps `updated_at` with its own clock. What does an incremental load need?
hint: Its rows arrive carrying a time three minutes in the past.

choices.text: An overlap longer than three minutes, so the window reaches its rows
choices.why: Right: the window has to reach back past the slowest clock.

choices.text: No change, since a watermark ignores the clock of the source
choices.why: The watermark is made of the source's own stamps.

choices.text: A full load every night instead, whatever the size of the table
choices.why: That works, at the price incremental loads exist to avoid.

choices.text: A uniqueness check at the door on `ride_id`
choices.why: The rows are missing, not doubled; nothing reaches the door.

prompt: The provider closes its statement's day in UTC; the copy closes it in `America/Sao_Paulo`. What does a nightly count show?
hint: Where does a payment at 22:30 in Curitiba fall?

choices.text: Agreement, since a count does not depend on a clock
choices.why: Which day a payment is counted on depends on the clock.

choices.text: A gap only on the nights when the clocks change for summer
choices.why: The gap is three hours wide every night.

choices.text: A gap every night, from the last three hours of it
choices.why: Right: the last three hours of each local day fall on the next UTC day.

choices.text: A gap of exactly one day's payments once a week
choices.why: The offset is three hours, not a day, and it repeats daily.

prompt: Roda Livre keeps the HMAC key in a secret store. Is the pseudonymised copy of the rides still personal data under the LGPD?
hint: Article 12, and who holds the key.

choices.text: No: a hash cannot be reversed, so it is anonymised
choices.why: Whoever has the key recomputes the stand-in and re-links it.

choices.text: Yes: anyone holding the key links it back to the customer
choices.why: Right: re-identifiable by reasonable means is still personal.

choices.text: No, once the phone column has been removed from the copy
choices.why: The pseudonym still points at one person, through the key.

choices.text: Only if the key is stored in the same database as the copy
choices.why: Keeping it apart lowers the harm of a leak, not the law's reach.

prompt: Which belong in the data contract with a source's owner? Choose all that apply.
hint: What a delivery can break.

choices.text: the columns a delivery carries
choices.why: Yes: a renamed column breaks the door.

choices.text: the count sent beside each file
choices.why: Yes: it is what the file check compares against.

choices.text: the limits a value must sit inside
choices.why: Yes: a rule the source does not know breaks when it changes.

choices.text: how often Marta's dashboard refreshes
choices.why: No: that is between the data team and its readers.
